newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU setback for Swedish alcohol monopoly.
newsitem.headline: EU setback for Swedish alcohol monopoly.

text.p: Sweden's state alcohol monopoly took a legal blow on Tuesday when an adviser at the European Court of Justice said European Union law was an "obstacle" to such retail sales regimes for alcohol.
The opinion of Advocate-General Michael Elmer represents a setback for Sweden, which has a monopoly on the retail sale of wines and spirits.
Opinions by the Advocates-General are only advisory, but are often followed by the court in final rulings.
The case comes after the district court of the Swedish town of Landskrona asked the EU court for a preliminary ruling on whether the monopoly over retail liquor sales was compatible with EU law.
The action was brought by the Landskrona public prosecutor against grocer Harry Franzen for breaking the monopoly of the state-owned Systembolaget over sales of wine and spirits.
Franzen started selling wine in his shop in 1994, determined to see if Sweden's stringent alcohol rules broke EU law.
He sold one-litre, sealed packs of white and red French, Italian and Spanish wines but he was soon ordered to stop by the police.
The Landskrona court had asked the EU court to rule on whether Swedish legislation met, for example, the EU's ban on quantitative restrictions on imports.

In his opinion, Elmer said EU legislation was an obstacle to national systems which give a state-owned company the sole right to all retail alcohol sales and which is the only lawful buyer of such beverages for the retail market.
"This (the opinion) is a complete victory for Harry Franzen," Ulf Bernitz, professor in European law at the Stockholm University, told the Swedish news agency.
